question: In its response to written question 002323/20261 from Gerald Hauser MEP, the EU Commission confirms that microplastics are harmful for both the environment and health. Whilst it claims that ‘plastic emissions from wind turbines are much lower than from other sources’, it does not refute the studies cited by Gerald Hauser MEP, according to which one wind turbine can shed up to 62 kg of microplastics annually.

Furthermore, the European Commission states that ‘assessment of the environmental impacts of offshore wind [has] also [been] addressed under Horizon Europe’. The EU project HORIZON-HLTH-2026-01-DISEASE-03, cited by the European Commission, focuses, amongst other things, on the long-term health effects of certain environmental and exposure factors.

The European Commission thus confirms, in an official document, a link between wind turbines and adverse health effects. Other EU projects also focus on further research into the massive impact of micro- and nanoplastics on human health, as well as environmental damage caused by offshore wind farms. 1.
Why has the Commission thus far studied only microplastic emissions from offshore wind farms, but not from onshore wind farms?
Why has the Commission so far failed to inform the public that wind turbines are causing massive microplastic pollution?
Why has the Commission so far failed to inform the public that wind turbines can have significant adverse impact on health?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) To the knowledge of the Commission, wind turbines are not causing ‘massive microplastic pollution’ or ‘significant adverse impact on health’. The Commission took note of the publication referred to in the written question E-002323/20261. However, it is not a scientific peer reviewed publication.

Scientific findings are most credible when they have been published in peer-reviewed journals2 and by that being relevant for evidence-based political decision-making. Renewable energy projects, including wind turbines, that have been developed and approved under EU and national environmental, health, planning and permitting rules make an important contribution to clean, secure and increasingly affordable energy.

Scientific evidence shows that wind and solar energy have among the lowest life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions of electricity generation technologies3 and provide a significant net societal benefit, including reduced air pollution, lower climate impacts and improved energy security4.
1 https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2026-002323_EN.html. 2 Independent peer review is the most direct means of ensuring quality. Before publication, experts not involved

in the work scrutinise the study design, data, analysis and conclusions, exposing methodological weaknesses and errors of interpretation. Beyond peer review, the evidentiary value of a study depends on the soundness of its methodology, including sample size, appropriate controls and the handling of bias and confounding factors.

It also depends on the transparency of its data and methods, the independence of its authors and funding, and the consistency of its findings with the wider literature. No single study is decisive, and evidence is best judged as a whole. Within that body of evidence, peer-reviewed studies that meet these standards carry greater weight than findings that have not undergone independent scrutiny.

3 The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Cambridge University Press, 2022), Chapter 6. 4 The International Energy Agency (IEA) - (2025), World Energy Outlook 2025, IEA, Paris https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-outlook-2025.
